newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan offer to be Asia middleman meets scepticism.
newsitem.headline: Japan offer to be Asia middleman meets scepticism.

text.p: A Japanese offer to promote links between its poorer Asian neighbours and the private sector has met with scepticism from some members of the Asian Development Bank who say cash is still the key.

Tokyo's proposal to explore new development strategies and act as an intermediary between Japanese business and ADB members was made at the bank's annual meeting, which ended in this southern Japanese city on Tuesday.

Tokyo, the largest stakeholder in the 56-member bank along with the United States, said it would maintain its leading role in the lending agency, but also called for cooperation over its new initiatives, unveiled by Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka at Sunday's opening session.

The proposals, touted by Japanese officials as the "main attraction" of Mitsuzuka's speech, were a plan to open an ADB Institute in Tokyo to "explore new development philosophies" and the "Fukuoka Dialogue" -- an opportunity for investment recipient countries to have "face-to-face" talks with Japan's private sector.
"As Asia's only developed nation, we must act as an intermediary between the private sector and our Asian neighbours," Mitsuzuka told his news conference on Sunday.
The aim is to promote private investment, in line with the ADB's goal of raising its profile as a catalyst in luring private capital into the region, Japanese officials said.

But some members, mindful of Mitsuzuka's other comment in the speech -- that Japan, faced with its own fiscal problems, may need to trim its development aid -- gave only conditional approval to the plan.
"We're supportive of the institute. But it (the effectiveness) would depend largely on the thinking of the Japanese policies and the ADB," Malaysia's Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim told Reuters.
Tokyo's blunt admission that it may have to be less generous with future aid was echoed by the United States, which said budgetary constraints in donor countries mandated more efficient operations.

"We look to the ADB to meet the high standards...with the basic objective of increasing their efficiency and effectiveness in a period of scarce budgetary funds," U.S. Treasury Senior Assistant Secretary Timothy Geithner said in a speech to the ADB meeting.
Aid recipients and newly graduated donors to the bank immediately bristled at the idea.

"We are concerned with the declining proportion of contributions from the donors' resources and would like to strongly urge traditional donors to share your wealth," Thai Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan said.

Countries such as Thailand and Malaysia have been borrowers from the bank but after recent economic success have become donors too -- and are irritated by the idea that wealthier members are backing off.
Japanese Finance Ministry officials said the specifics of new proposals had still to be decided.
"First of all, we need to see whether we can get people -- researchers -- for the institute," said one official.
He also admitted that the Fukuoka Dialogue idea of helping to promote Japanese investment overseas was nothing new, noting the existence of the Japan External Trade Organisation (JETRO).
Although its initiatives failed to impress, Japan's presence was felt in one of the hottest issues at the three-day meeting -- one which was not on the agenda.
An application by North Korea to join the ADB was the focal point of backroom discussions, delegates said.

Membership of the bank, sought by many poor nations seeking a shot in the arm for their economies, was not on the official agenda as annual meetings are not intended for discussion of such a specific topic, ADB officials said.
Japan, a key player in the debate over Pyongyang's membership, kept a low profile on the issue.
"We need to consider it carefully," Mitsuzuka said. "We must take into account the judgement of our diplomatic authorities, and also consult with other nations."
Japan, which does not have diplomatic ties with North Korea, is said to be blocking its inclusion into the ADB.
Japan has accused North Korean agents of abducting Japanese citizens in the past and has been reluctant to provide food aid to Pyongyang as a result.
